name: AML / transaction monitoring (near-real-time and event-batch)
parent_research_topic: Beava use cases — current and potential applications of beava as a real-time feature server

domain_fit.domain_name: Anti-Money-Laundering (AML) transaction monitoring and Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) detection
domain_fit.one_line_definition: A bank, EMI, money-transmitter, crypto exchange or PSP's AML / financial-crime team must, within seconds-to-hours of each transaction, score every customer-counterparty flow for structuring, mule-network, peer-group-anomaly, sudden-cross-border and other AML typologies in order to raise auditable alerts that feed regulator-facing SAR/CTR/STR filings, not to auto-block the payment.
domain_fit.representative_jobs_to_be_done: 1) Detect classical AML typologies — structuring (deposits clustered just below the CTR/SAR threshold over rolling 7–60 day windows), smurfing (one source fanning out to many sub-threshold accounts), rapid in/rapid-out, dormant-account-wake, sudden cross-border activity and amount/time-of-day anomalies — and convert them into alerts a Level-1 investigator can triage. 2) Compute peer-group features (customer's activity vs. their segment's distribution of count, sum, distinct-counterparties, geography) so the rules engine and ML scorer can flag step-outs from peer behaviour rather than fire on raw absolute thresholds. 3) Identify mule-network indicators (first-seen-account becoming a fan-in node, dormant-wake, multi-hop pass-through, behavioural shift in dormant accounts) and link them to graph-side investigations. 4) Pre-compute and serve the feature vector that the bank's scoring engine and case-management system can re-fetch at decision time and again at audit-time, so a regulator can ask 'what feature values triggered this SAR on 2026-02-14T14:32:07Z?' and the answer is reproducible.
domain_fit.event_shapes: Wire / ACH / SWIFT / SEPA / FedNow / RTP / UPI / pacs.008 / pacs.002 payment events; cash deposit and withdrawal events (currency_in, currency_out with denomination); cheque clearings; card transactions; remittance/MSB sends and receives; for crypto exchanges: on-chain deposit, on-chain withdrawal, fiat-on-ramp, fiat-off-ramp, internal-transfer, address_first_seen. Common fields: timestamp, account_id, counterparty_account, counterparty_bank/PSP/VASP, amount, currency, channel (branch/ATM/online/mobile/API/teller), country_from, country_to, MCC/purpose_code, beneficiary_first_seen_ts, customer_segment, KYC_risk_tier, sanctions_check_status, end_to_end_id. For crypto: tx_hash, from_address, to_address, chain_id, asset, deposit_risk_score (from Chainalysis/TRM/Elliptic), exposure_category. KYC/CDD update events (customer_segment_change, employment_change, expected_volume_band) also land as state-update events.
domain_fit.feature_shapes: Counters and sums per account and per (account+counterparty) pair: count(cash_deposits, window=1d/7d/30d), sum(amount, window) per customer, count(distinct counterparty_account, 30d/90d), count(transactions < $10000 in 7d), ratio(below_threshold_count / total_count). Velocities: transactions/hour, transactions/day, amount/day per (customer, channel, country). First-seen / dormant-wake flags: time_since_last_activity, is_first_transaction_to_country, days_since_account_open, days_since_first_high_value_transaction. Distributions and z-scores: amount vs customer's 90-day baseline, amount vs peer-group segment baseline (t-digest / quantile sketch), hour-of-day percentile per customer. Distinct-counterparty cardinality (HLL acceptable for >24h windows). Fan-in / fan-out: distinct sources to an account in 24h/7d, distinct sinks from an account in 24h/7d. Geo / corridor features: distinct countries in 30d, sum-of-amounts per (customer, country, 30d), is_high_risk_jurisdiction join. Mostly multi-window sliding (1d, 7d, 30d, 90d) and tumbling (calendar-day, calendar-month for CTR aggregation); session windows are less common than in fraud.
domain_fit.entity_grain: Multiple parallel grains, with the customer as the primary regulator-facing entity. Typical keys: (customer_id), (account_id), (account+counterparty) pair, (customer, channel), (customer, country_corridor), (counterparty_account) — including external counterparties seen as fan-in nodes. For crypto: (customer_id), (deposit_address), (withdrawal_address), (counterparty_address). For peer-group features the grain is (customer_segment_id) holding the segment-level distribution baseline. For corridor / typology rules, (country_from, country_to, customer_segment) is a useful aggregate grain. The (account+counterparty) pair is especially important for structuring and pass-through detection.
domain_fit.window_semantics_required: Predominantly sliding windows over long horizons: 1d, 7d, 30d, 90d (and increasingly 180d/365d for SAR-quality typologies and ongoing-monitoring under EU AMLR and FFIEC). Tumbling calendar-day and calendar-month windows are required for CTR aggregation (the $10k/calendar-day rule under 31 CFR is calendar-based, not rolling). Hopping windows (e.g. 30d hopping by 1d) are common for peer-group baselines. Approximate sketches (HLL for distinct-counterparty count, CMS for heavy-hitters, t-digest / KLL for amount quantiles) are acceptable for everything except the regulator-driven exact thresholds (CTR $10k, structuring just-below-threshold counts, mandatory reporting thresholds in other jurisdictions) which must be exact. Session windows are rare; the natural unit is the customer-day or customer-month.
domain_fit.exactly_once_or_idempotency_needs: Strict idempotency required. Re-publishing or replaying the same payment event must not double-count a CTR-aggregate amount or a structuring counter; investigators and regulators will ask the system to reproduce the alert from the underlying events, and SAR supporting documentation must reconcile to the feature values. Upstream at-least-once delivery is the norm (Kafka/Kinesis), so the feature server should dedupe on (transaction_id / end_to_end_id / tx_hash).

technical_fit.latency_budget: Wider than fraud. AML alerts are case-managed rather than auto-blocking, so end-to-end alert-generation latency tolerances are typically seconds-to-minutes (real-time / near-real-time) and in legacy stacks hours (overnight batch). Feature read p99 for online scoring is generously budgeted at 50–500 ms; vendor positioning (Hawk, Flagright) cites sub-300 ms full-pipeline including sanctions screening, and Hawk claims a 150 ms average response time. For on-rail blocking (sanctions screening) and instant-payment AML the budget tightens to the rail's full SLA (10 s SEPA Instant, ~20 s FedNow/RTP). Beava's sub-millisecond TCP get / batch_get is far inside any AML tolerance and would mostly be limited by upstream ETL.
technical_fit.feature_freshness_sla: Mixed and typology-dependent. Velocity / structuring features must reflect the just-arrived transaction (effective freshness ~0 ms, same-event update-and-read) to fire while the customer is still in-channel. Peer-group baselines and 90/180/365-day distributions can tolerate hours of staleness — they are recomputed nightly or on a 1h cadence. Customer-risk-tier / KYC fields can tolerate up to a day. Sanctions-list joins must be refreshed on every list update (EU IPR / AMLR daily expectation). For SAR-quality monitoring, regulators care more that the value at decision time is reproducible than that it is sub-second fresh.
technical_fit.throughput_profile: Highly heterogeneous. A mid-tier US community bank may see tens-to-low-hundreds of EPS across all rails; a top-tier global bank or major card-acquiring PSP may see tens of thousands of EPS; a top crypto exchange sees thousands-to-tens-of-thousands of on-chain + fiat events per second across hundreds of millions of addresses (Chainalysis maps >1B addresses; Elliptic handles >2M screenings/month with sub-second 'Holistic'); Hawk and Flagright cite monitoring billions of transactions cumulatively with sub-second latencies. Beava's published ~684k EPS on a single Apple-M4 core (TCP+msgpack, parallel=16) is comfortably above any single-tenant AML steady-state and leaves ample headroom for 20–200 feature lookups per decision. [uncertain] — per-buyer EPS is not publicly disclosed at the bank level.
technical_fit.read_to_write_ratio: Balanced to read-heavy. Each transaction is one event-write but produces dozens of feature reads for rules + ML scoring + case-investigator dashboards (which re-fetch features when an analyst opens a case). Reads dominate by roughly 20–100x in production AML stacks, with investigator-side re-fetching adding additional read amplification.
technical_fit.state_size_estimate: For a mid-tier bank: ~5–20M customers × ~10–50 KB per-customer feature state (multi-window counters, distinct-counterparty HLL, amount quantile sketches, country-corridor maps, peer-group baseline pointers, dormant-wake flags) ~= 0.05–1 TB hot working set. For a top-tier global bank or large card network: 100M–1B entities × similar bytes/entity, exploding to 1–50 TB once (account+counterparty) and (counterparty external) pair grains are included; many pairs are inactive and amenable to TTL eviction. For a top crypto exchange or analytics provider, address-grain cardinality is in the 100M–1B+ range. Beava's in-memory-only model fits a mid-tier bank's hot working set on a beefy node; top-tier banks and large crypto exchanges will exceed single-node RAM and need sharding or tiered storage. [uncertain] — bytes/entity is an order-of-magnitude planning estimate.
technical_fit.cardinality_pattern: Mixed. Customer / account cardinality grows slowly with onboarding (bounded by KYC). Counterparty external cardinality is explosive and unbounded (every external bank, every external crypto address seen). (Account+counterparty) pair grain is explosive in the long tail but bounded per customer. Country-corridor cardinality is small (~200 countries × ~200 countries = ~40k corridors). Peer-group segments are small and bounded (typically 10–500 segments). Crypto address-grain is essentially unbounded.
technical_fit.typical_state_lifecycle_and_ttl: Long. Short-window counters (1d/7d/30d) need ~30 day TTL. Behavioural baselines and peer-group distributions: 90–365 days rolling, refreshed nightly. Dormant-wake detection needs at least 90 days of last-activity timestamps. Structuring features benefit from 60–90 day lookbacks. Regulatory record retention is 5 years (BSA / 31 CFR 1010.430, EU AMLR 5y) for SAR supporting documentation, but this is satisfied by archiving the WAL + decision log to cold storage; the live feature server only holds the hot working set. Note: the hot live state for AML is materially longer-lived than for fraud (months vs hours-to-days), which stresses any in-memory feature store.
technical_fit.typical_feature_count_per_decision: 30–200+ per transaction. AML scoring stacks query multi-window counters across many entity grains plus peer-group baselines, dormant-wake flags, corridor risk, sanctions joins and prior-alert history. Investigator case-review re-fetches a similar or larger vector. batch_get / pipelined-reads are essential.
technical_fit.durability_requirements: Regulator-grade. BSA/AML (US, 31 CFR 1010.430), FFIEC examination expectations, FinCEN SAR/CTR requirements, EU AMLR (applies 10 July 2027), EU AMLA (operational 1 July 2025), AMLD6, FCA / FCA-handbook (UK), FINTRAC (Canada), MAS (Singapore), FATF Recommendation 11 — all require records retained for 5 years (in some jurisdictions 7) and reproducible at audit. Beava's WAL + periodic snapshot is crash-safe but is not the system-of-record; the bank's core banking / payment-rail archive is. Beava's role is reproducible-derived-feature serving; the 5-7 year retention is satisfied by archiving the upstream event log and the decision log. The 'refuse on network-FS' default is the right guardrail. Regulators will, however, expect: (i) point-in-time / as-of feature reads, (ii) per-read audit log (who-asked-what-when), (iii) hot-standby so a node loss doesn't drop 90+ days of behavioural baseline, (iv) deterministic replay from WAL.
technical_fit.deployment_topology_fit: Single-binary-per-region is workable for a mid-tier bank or an EMI / money-transmitter / mid-tier crypto exchange. Top-tier global banks and large crypto exchanges need multi-region active-active for resilience and data-residency (EU AMLR / GDPR push EU data on-EU), which beava does not natively provide in v0. Sidecar-to-existing-AML-platform (Actimize, Hawk, Quantexa, SymphonyAI, Flagright, Verafin) is a realistic adoption path — beava becomes the low-latency feature substrate underneath the incumbent's rules / case-management UI. Beava's lack of in-process sharding caps single-tenant scale at one node; the long state-lifecycle and large per-customer state make sharding more pressing for AML than for fraud.

commercial_fit.who_buys: Financial-crime / AML / compliance engineering teams inside banks, credit unions, EMIs, neobanks, money-transmitters, remittance corridors, MSBs, crypto exchanges and VASPs; ML / data-platform teams at large institutions running in-house monitoring; the AML-platform vendors themselves (Hawk, Flagright, ComplyAdvantage, Lucinity, Unit21, Sardine, Napier, Tookitaki, AMLYZE, Salv, Castellum.AI) who could embed beava as a feature substrate; and regtech startups building niche typology detectors. RegOps and Money-Laundering-Reporting-Officer (MLRO) functions own the budget; engineering owns the build.
commercial_fit.market_size_signal: Large and structurally regulator-pulled. The global AML software market is forecast at USD ~4.1B in 2025 growing to USD ~9.4B by 2030 (MarketsandMarkets). The broader transaction-monitoring market is sized at USD 16–20B in 2025 (Mordor / SNS Insider, definitions vary) and forecast to USD 47.6B by 2033 (SNS Insider). US AML enforcement penalties exceeded $940M in 2025 alone (Wolters Kluwer reporting). Industry-wide, 85–95% of alerts are false positives (Everest Group benchmark; widely cited 95–98% in rule-based systems) meaning the marginal value of better features (especially peer-group baselines and behavioural baselines) is enormous. Public vendor scale: Hawk monitors billions of transactions globally; Feedzai raised $100M in Oct 2023; Chainalysis maps over 1B addresses and serves 9 of the top 10 crypto exchanges; Featurespace (Visa-owned) processes ~100B payments/year. [uncertain] — individual vendor revenues are not publicly disclosed.
commercial_fit.urgency_drivers: 1) EU AMLR / AMLA / AMLD6 — AMLA operational 1 July 2025; AMLR and AMLD6 apply from 10 July 2027 — every EU credit institution, EMI, crypto VASP, and many digital platforms must re-tool their transaction monitoring against new technical standards expected through 2026. 2) EU Instant Payments Regulation forces AML/sanctions screening inside 10s for SEPA Instant (mandatory acceptance Jan 2025, mandatory sending Oct 2025). 3) FinCEN's expansion of BSA/AML obligations to RIAs (effective 2028) opens a new buyer cohort. 4) US AML / OFAC enforcement penalties ($940M in 2025) and headline-making bank consent orders. 5) Regulator-driven 'real-time mule and APP-fraud reimbursement' regimes (UK PSR Oct 2024) push AML and fraud-platform convergence ('FRAML'). 6) FATF Recommendation 11 / 15 / 16 updates pushing on cross-border + crypto reporting. 7) High false-positive rates (85–95%) drive every CFO of every bank to look for ML/feature-quality upgrades. 8) AMLA Work Programme 2025 publishing up-to-23 Level-2/Level-3 measures by 10 July 2026.
commercial_fit.regulatory_or_audit_constraints: Heavy. US: BSA / 31 CFR 1010.430 (5-year retention), FinCEN SAR rules (30-day initial-detection-to-filing window, $5k SAR threshold, $10k CTR threshold), OFAC sanctions, FFIEC examination manual. EU: AMLR (applies 10 Jul 2027), AMLA (operational 1 Jul 2025), AMLD6, EU IPR Art. 5d daily customer-base sanctions screening, GDPR (data minimisation, right to erasure tension with 5-year retention), PSD3/PSR (2027 application). UK: MLR 2017 (as amended), FCA SYSC, PSR APP-reimbursement (Oct 2024). Crypto-specific: FATF Travel Rule (R.16), MiCA (EU), CARF. Singapore MAS Notice 626, Hong Kong AMLO, Canada FINTRAC PCMLTFA, Australia AUSTRAC AML/CTF Act, India PMLA. Data: GDPR / DPDP / CCPA. PCI-DSS if card data co-resident. All push toward: (i) reproducible features at decision time, (ii) immutable audit log, (iii) 5-year-plus retention of supporting documentation, (iv) data-residency controls.
commercial_fit.time_to_value_signal: 1–2 weeks for a velocity + structuring + dormant-wake demo against synthetic or open AML datasets (e.g. PaySim, IBM AML synthetic dataset). 1–3 months for a shadow-mode deployment alongside an incumbent platform with full peer-group baselines. 6–18 months for regulator-grade production cutover (model validation under SR 11-7 / EBA validation guidelines, MLRO sign-off, SOC2 / ISO 27001, runbook for WAL+snapshot recovery, independent testing per FFIEC). AML buyers' procurement cycles are slower than fraud's and bias toward established vendors; open-source / Apache-2.0 is attractive for in-house builds but requires the buyer's compliance team to validate it themselves.

competition.incumbents: Generic streaming / feature-store stacks deployed under AML systems today: Apache Flink for stateful stream processing of long-horizon counters (peer-group baselines, structuring windows) — widely cited as the Tier-1 streaming engine in U.S. payment networks; Redis Enterprise / Cluster used as a low-latency feature cache by some banks (also referenced as a real-time decisioning store, e.g. ~700k TPS reported by a top-3 card network); Aerospike for sub-ms feature serving (PayPal, Barclays, Forter publicly cited migration from Redis+Couchbase to Aerospike); Apache Cassandra / ScyllaDB for historical-pattern storage; ksqlDB and Kafka Streams for in-Kafka aggregation; Tecton, Feast, Hopsworks, Fennel, Chalk as ML feature stores. Open-source AML-specific decision engines that overlap beava's territory: Jube (AGPLv3, real-time AML+fraud, explicitly architects in-memory frequently-accessed state for sub-ms decisioning) and Marble (open-source real-time decision engine for fraud and AML, On-Prem / SaaS deployable). The dominant production pattern is 'Kafka + Flink + Redis-or-Aerospike + scoring engine + case management UI'.
competition.competitive_incumbent_per_domain: NICE Actimize (Nasdaq-owned suite of ~280+ predefined AML rules, modular suspicious-activity / sanctions / fraud), Oracle FCCM, SAS AML, FICO TONBELLER Siron, IBM Safer Payments / IBM Financial Crimes Insight, FIS, BAE Systems NetReveal, ACI Worldwide, Fiserv, Verafin (Nasdaq, US community-bank-heavy with explicit mule-detection product). RegTech entrants: ComplyAdvantage Mesh, Hawk (Hawk.AI — '150 ms average response, false-positive reduction by 70%' positioning), Flagright (no-code, sub-300 ms screening), Lucinity (gen-AI case manager 'Luci'), Unit21 (agentic AI), Sardine (KYC + AML + fraud convergence, $70M Series C), Napier AI, Tookitaki, SymphonyAI Sensa, Silent Eight, Castellum.AI, Salv, AMLYZE, Fenergo. Network / graph specialists: Quantexa (Entity Resolution + Network Generation + Graph Analytics + AI pillars; HSBC, Standard Chartered, BNY Mellon publicly cited), Linkurious, TigerGraph, Neo4j. Crypto-specific: Chainalysis (KYT/Reactor/Storyline, 9 of top-10 exchanges), TRM Labs (sub-second API, 100+ chains, 45+ chain tracing), Elliptic (Holistic, 2B+ labeled addresses, sub-second), Solidus Labs, Nominis, Scorechain. Beava would slot underneath one of these as the feature substrate; it does not replace the rules-authoring UI, the case-manager, the SAR-filing connector, the sanctions-list maintenance, or the graph engine.
competition.beava_differentiator: 1) Single-binary, Apache-2.0, no broker / no ETL — a credible 'Redis-for-stateful-features with 50+ aggregation primitives' positioning is attractive to AML-platform vendors who today stitch Kafka+Flink+Redis under their UI and want to embed a smaller substrate. 2) Declarative @bv.event / @bv.table primitives express structuring, velocity, distinct-counterparty, peer-group z-score, fan-in/fan-out as schema rather than Flink jobs + Lua scripts. 3) ~684k EPS on a single core gives huge headroom over per-bank steady-state and supports the 30–200 feature reads per decision plus investigator re-fetch amplification. 4) Atomic per-event update-and-read fits the AML rule 'this transaction must update the structuring counter before being scored against the threshold'. 5) HTTP/JSON + framed TCP (JSON or msgpack) lets the bank's existing rules engine, Python scorer, or third-party AML platform call beava directly. 6) Apache-2.0, no open-core, no per-tenant SaaS lock-in — important for AML-platform vendors who reject mixed licences and for in-house bank builds. 7) WAL + snapshot with refuse-on-network-FS is the right default for a regulated buyer who would otherwise quietly run on NFS and break crash recovery.
competition.where_beava_loses_today: 1) No TLS — disqualifying for any regulated AML deployment without an in-front mTLS-terminating proxy; even with one, most AML teams want mTLS to the feature store itself. 2) No authn/authz / RBAC — every regulated buyer needs per-tenant tokens, per-role access, and per-team audit. 3) No in-process sharding — caps single-tenant scale at one node, which is a hard limit for top-tier banks given AML's long state-lifecycle (90–365 day baselines). 4) No hot-standby / replication — losing 90+ days of behavioural baseline on a crash, even with WAL replay, is unacceptable to most AML/MLRO teams. 5) In-memory only — AML's long lookbacks (peer-group baselines, dormant-wake detection up to 180–365 days) push state size beyond comfortable single-node RAM for large buyers; tiered storage (RAM -> SSD) is needed. 6) No native point-in-time / as-of read — regulators expect 'what was the feature value at decision time' to be answerable on demand. 7) No native sanctions / PEP / adverse-media list integration — every competitor ships this. 8) No graph / entity-resolution layer — Quantexa, Linkurious, TigerGraph, Neo4j own mule-ring discovery. 9) No case-management UI / no SAR-narrative generator — Lucinity / Unit21 / Sardine / Verafin own this entire workflow. 10) No triggers / no webhook on threshold-cross — AML teams want 'fire when structuring score > k' emitted by the feature server. 11) No multi-tenancy — AML-platform vendors wanting to embed beava on behalf of many banks would need either per-tenant binaries or a namespace + sharding story. 12) No native idempotency keys on push — required for at-least-once upstream rails to avoid double-counting CTR aggregates.
competition.integration_surface: Banks: Kafka, IBM MQ, vendor-specific buses, FedLine / FedNow API, SWIFT MX, EBA RT1 / TIPS, NPCI UPI Switch, core-banking change-data-capture (Goldengate, Debezium). EMIs and neobanks: Kafka, REST, Temporal. Crypto exchanges: in-house tx-firehose, ChainalysisKYT webhooks, TRM Labs API push, Elliptic Holistic API. Most modern AML feature stores are Kafka-consumer-shaped (Tecton/Feast/Hopsworks/Fennel), while beava is HTTP/TCP push-shaped — this is unusual in the AML stack. The natural beava integration is either (a) a thin Kafka-to-beava-TCP sidecar, or (b) direct ingestion from the bank's payment-orchestration / core-banking event bus (HTTP/REST is increasingly common). gRPC support would close a recognised gap with Tecton/Chalk and help banks that standardise on gRPC internally. Outbound to the AML-platform rules / case-management UI is via batch_get HTTP, which is well-fit.
competition.scoring_engine_coupling: Both. Production AML stacks always run rules-and-ML in parallel: rule engines (Drools, OpenRules, FEEL, vendor DSLs inside Actimize/Hawk/Flagright/Napier) on top of features, and ML scorers (XGBoost, LightGBM, ONNX, isolation-forest, graph neural nets via Quantexa) on the same features. Beava is feature-serving only; the buyer plugs it into both pipelines.

adoption_signals.adversarial_pressure_level: High but slower-tempo than payments-fraud. AML adversaries iterate over weeks-to-months (designing mule networks, rotating shell companies, shifting corridors), not minutes; feature drift is real but slower than payments-fraud feature drift. The case-managed (not auto-blocked) workflow means the cost of a missed alert is regulator action and fines, not immediate consumer loss — so adversaries have more headroom to evade. Sanctions-evasion and crypto-mixer adversaries (Tornado Cash and successors) iterate faster on the crypto side. Net: adversarial pressure is high-but-bounded, well above analytics/observability but below ad-fraud or anti-cheat.

risk_and_non_goals.non_goals: 1) Full event archive / 5–7 year regulator-grade retention of raw transactions — that belongs in a warehouse (Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks Delta Lake, S3 Glacier) plus a SoR archive; beava holds derived features. 2) Historical batch backfill of multi-year transaction history for typology back-testing — Spark / Flink batch / Snowflake territory, not beava's. 3) Case-management UI, alert-disposition workflow, SAR/CTR narrative generation, regulator e-filing — owned by Lucinity, Unit21, Sardine, Verafin, NICE Actimize, Hawk, Flagright, etc. 4) Entity resolution, graph-based mule-ring discovery, cross-entity link analysis — owned by Quantexa, TigerGraph, Neo4j, Linkurious. 5) Sanctions / PEP / adverse-media list maintenance — buy from ComplyAdvantage, Castellum.AI, Refinitiv World-Check, Dow Jones, LexisNexis. 6) On-chain risk labelling — buy from Chainalysis, TRM Labs, Elliptic. 7) Model training, model registry, model validation under SR 11-7 — Vertex / SageMaker / Databricks / MLflow / domino. 8) System-of-record for KYC, customer-segment assignments, or risk-tier — those live in the core banking system.
risk_and_non_goals.open_engineering_gaps: To be production-grade for any regulated AML buyer, beava would need (roughly decreasing priority): (1) TLS termination (mTLS preferred) — non-negotiable; (2) authn/authz with RBAC and per-tenant namespaces (OIDC/SAML for admin); (3) per-read audit log (who-asked-what-when) — directly required for AML reproducibility under FFIEC / EU AMLR; (4) point-in-time / as-of feature reads ('what was structuring_count_30d for customer X at 14:32:07Z on 2026-02-14?') — directly required for SAR reproducibility; (5) hot-standby / synchronous-WAL replication so a node loss does not drop 90–365 day behavioural baselines; (6) in-process sharding or a documented horizontal-scale story (consistent-hash router, replication, failover) — necessary for top-tier banks given the long state-lifecycle; (7) per-feature TTL and tiered storage (RAM -> local SSD) so 90–365 day baselines can outlast RAM; (8) idempotency tokens on push (dedupe by transaction_id / end_to_end_id / tx_hash) — required for at-least-once upstream rails to avoid double-counting CTR / structuring aggregates; (9) triggers / 'fire-on-threshold-cross' webhooks so the feature server can emit alerts directly into the case-management UI; (10) gRPC surface in addition to HTTP/TCP; (11) secondary indexes for ad-hoc investigation queries ('show all accounts with >5 distinct counterparties + sum>$50k in 7d'); (12) deterministic replay from WAL with verifiable hashes (regulators want to recompute alerts from raw events); (13) multi-tenancy so AML-platform vendors can embed beava across many bank customers; (14) Kafka-consumer source / sink connector so beava drops into the dominant 'Kafka + Flink + Redis' stack; (15) native sanctions / PEP / adverse-media list lookup hook; (16) Prometheus + OpenTelemetry exporters for feature-drift / data-quality monitoring; (17) data-residency controls (EU-only RAM, US-only RAM) for GDPR / EU AMLR / regional regulators; (18) GDPR right-to-erasure surface (delete-by-customer-id) that does not corrupt aggregate counters — a non-trivial design issue for any feature store.
risk_and_non_goals.trigger_action_required: Yes — AML teams want event-driven actions from the feature store ('emit STRUCTURING_ALERT when count(deposits < $10k in 30d) >= N AND sum_below_threshold_ratio > p'; 'emit DORMANT_WAKE when days_since_last_activity > 90 AND sum_in_24h > customer_baseline * k'). Beava today is feature-serving only, so the caller's rule engine has to poll-and-threshold. Adding a trigger / webhook surface (or a 'fire when atomic counter crosses threshold' primitive) is one of the highest-leverage adds for this domain, second only to TLS+authn.
